metadata.title: When Is a Claude Legal Memo Actually Reliable?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether a Claude-drafted legal memo that cites real cases and reads confidently is ready to rely on, or only once every citation is checked. Lands the carry-out that a memo is reliable once its citations are verified, not the moment it's drafted.

beats.narration_text: Someone types 'OPINION' and hesitates. That's the whole confusion. A legal opinion is a lawyer's final call. A memo is a draft analysis, unverified. Different documents. Different weight. Liam, in for Bear.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening with a memo that reads clean. The model was optimized to produce fluent, well-cited legal analysis — that's exactly what you see. But fluency isn't currency. Take a citation that names a real case, correctly, by name and by holding — and imagine that case got overruled last year. The memo can't know. It writes the dead citation with the same confidence it writes every live one. They optimized for coherence at the expense of currency, and it works if you value a clean draft; it fails if you need a verified answer. Every citation is a claim that has to be checked before it counts.

shot.new_visual_element: A memo page dense with citations; one citation gets circled in accent, then struck, with a caption revealing why

production_viz.label: A confident citation, quietly dead
production_viz.mechanic: A memo page densely filled with citation lines. One line reading a real-looking case citation gets circled in accent color, then struck through as a caption fades in below: 'overruled last year.' The page's border flashes accent, not from an error in the drafting, but from what almost got relied on as if it were still good law.

beats.narration_text: A memo handoff that actually works has three moving parts. First, the question and facts going in, structured. Second, the analysis coming back in the classic shape — issue, rule, application, conclusion. Third — the part most people skip — a verification pass, before the memo counts as anything at all. Watch the anchor. Same memo, back, with one citation stamped in the margin. Not confirmed. Flagged to check.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three labeled parts lighting in turn (question / draft / verify), then a memo page stamped FLAGGED -- VERIFY

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three parts, then the memo page
production_viz.mechanic: Three chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a part of a working memo handoff (question / draft / verify), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A clean, short memo page appears -- issue, rule, application, conclusion, one citation line visible -- with a stamp across the margin reading 'FLAGGED -- VERIFY' in bold. THIS EXACT PAGE RETURNS, CONFIRMED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That flagged citation gets pulled and checked against the law as it stands today. Only when every citation clears does the document promote from draft to something an attorney can actually lean on. Now name the two failure modes. A citation with no flag is not the same as a confirmed citation — the flag is a request, not a warranty, and someone still has to look at every line. And a memo that comes back heavily corrected isn't the system failing — that's the verification step doing exactly the job it was put there to do.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the flagged citation gets checked and the memo is stamped VERIFIED -- RELIABLE; then splits into 'no flag is not confirmed' and 'corrected is not failure'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- flagged, then verified
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 MEMO PAGE RETURNS, identical placement, its 'FLAGGED -- VERIFY' stamp crossed out and replaced with a checkmark and a new stamp reading 'VERIFIED -- RELIABLE'. It splits into two cards: left reads 'no flag shown' with a struck-through 'CONFIRMED' beneath it labelled 'no flag is not confirmed'; right reads 'heavily corrected' with a checkmark beneath it labelled 'corrected is not failure'.

beats.narration_text: A memo isn't reliable because it reads confidently. It's reliable once every citation in it has been checked.

props.quote: A memo isn't reliable because it reads confidently. It's reliable once every citation in it has been checked.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no CLI, nothing installed. Take a real legal question you're working on. Ask for an issue-rule-application-conclusion memo, with every case citation flagged so you can verify it. Read the flags. Check each cited case against the law as it stands today. Then, and only then, does the memo count. Go deeper: which citations most often go dead between when a memo is drafted and when it's relied on — overruled, superseded, or distinguished — and how would you catch each class before it slips into a filing? Liam, in for Bear.
